segments.text: A Proactive Risk Anticipation and Multi-Agent Orchestration Algorithm for Benchmarking Clinical AR Assistants in the AR-ClinAgent Framework Abstract-Augmented Reality (AR)–assisted clinical systems are increasingly being adopted to support healthcare professionals during complex procedural workflows; however, the absence of a unified evaluation standard continues to limit their reliability, safety validation, and scalability. To overcome this limitation, the AR-ClinAgent framework is introduced as a benchmark and assessment platform applicable to both simulation laboratories and manikin-based clinical environments. The framework operates through a structured perception-to-action cycle that involves capturing egocentric video input, retrieving clinically validated procedural steps through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounding, planning and executing context-specific actions, rendering real-time AR overlays for clinician guidance, verifying procedural outcomes, and logging detailed performance metrics for assessment. A major advancement within this framework is the integration of Proactive Risk Anticipation (PRA) and Multi-Agent Orchestration, which enables predictive error detection and intelligent task division among specialized AI sub-agents to enhance workflow reliability and operational efficiency. The platform employs privacy-preserving, high-stakes clinical datasets focused on ultrasound-guided intravenous access, central line insertion, and medication verification, ensuring both realism and compliance. Evaluation metrics include procedural accuracy, latency, intervention frequency, safety incidents, and energy consumption, enabling a multi-dimensional analysis of system performance. Baseline experiments show that PRA-empowered AR agents reduce clinical oversight interventions by 31%, improve step-wise execution accuracy by 26%, and decrease near-miss incidents by 22% compared to non-predictive systems, while latency is lowered by 18% and device-level energy usage improves by 14% due to distributed task processing. With its standardized schemas, scoring mechanisms, and reproducible baselines, AR-ClinAgent establishes a reliable foundation for fair comparisons between AR-assistant models, providing explicit insight into the trade-offs between safety and efficiency. By combining regulated procedural grounding with anticipatory intelligence, the framework accelerates the evolution of trustworthy AR assistants, advancing their readiness for seamless integration into real-world clinical practice. The use of AR application with clinical workflows supports overlay guidance during high-risk procedures (central-line insertion, ultrasound-guided intravenous access and medication

Whilst positive results have been shown in simulation-based settings, current AR-assisted approaches suffer from several shortcomings such as failure to ensure procedural consistency, over-delayed interventions and lack of common evaluation frameworks [5][6]. Conventional subjective evaluation and small scale of objective performance metrics are used in most assessment techniques that do not present a holistic view to the procedural dynamics which are as dynamic and context-specific [7][8]. The lack of this discrepancy has slowed the scalability, reproducibility and regulatory validation in AR-assisted technologies [9][10]. Recently, some AI-based methods have attempted to cope with workflow optimization or error reduction but few frameworks have comprehensively considered proactive risk anticipation and cognitive task allocation in terms of specialized sub-agents [11][12]. Bridging this gap calls for a coherent framework that can assess AR assistants in controlled yet realistic clinical settings, while considering both safety-critical results and the system efficiency. It is well-known that the PRA can significantly contribute to reducing errors and improve procedural consistency in clinical AI systems 13. PRA and its pre-emptive failure prediction work as an early warning system enabling interventions to be introduced early enough, decreasing near misses [15][16]. As a PRA variant, multi-agent orchestration seeks to partition various cognitive and perceptual tasks among specialized AI sub-agents with the expectation of saving system latency and energy consumption at the expense of high accuracy [17][18]. This combination of characteristics could be implemented in AR-assisted systems for real-time adjustment to different clinical scenarios with reliable responsiveness and patient safety [19][20]. The MenTOR framework draws together RAG-based procedural grounding, egocentric perception and AR overlay delivery to create a structured process of perception leading to action, which supports correct task performance following clinically approved guidelines. This integration also allows performance metrics to be logged in real time for quantitative benchmarking, yielding a benchmark standard by which AR assistants can be evaluated within simulation- and manikin-based scenarios. Assessment of AR-assisted systems cannot be limited to completion rate only — but rather that a multivariate approach must be used, including intervention counts, safety incident counts, latency and energy efficiency [1][3][5]. Pioneering studies have shown that predictive AR systems with PRA mechanisms can decrease the clinical supervision interventions by more than 30% and increase step-wise procedural precision by 25–30% [6][7]. It has also been demonstrated that multi- agent orchestration can improve resource assignment, minimise device-level energy usage and continue to support real-time behaviour under highly complex behaviours [8][9]. These findings emphasize the requirement for minimal benchmarking that also considers the intricate balance of safety, efficiency and usability in AR-based clinical environments. In addition, we require standardized datasets and scoring protocols to permit reproducibility, inter-system comparison, and regulatory scrutiny 10. Moreover, these frameworks can provide insights into design tradeoffs by revealing when optimizing for predictive accuracy or latency results in the best patient centered workflow. The AR-ClinAgent framework addresses these limitations by integrating PRA, multi-agent orchestration with RAG-based grounding and real-time AR overlays [12][13][14]. It serves as a benchmark for intubation accuracy, intubation time-lag, the number of attempts involved in the process, complications such as safety incidents and energy expenditure in a vast range of

segments.text: high performance environments [15][16]. By collecting egocentric data and imitating lifelike clinical scenarios, the network allows for the validation of systems in a robust way as well as privacy compliance and clinical practices [17][18]. Especially, this work (1) sets forth a common benchmark for AR-assisted clinical assistants, (2) introduces PRA mechanisms and multi-agent orchestration to enhance safety, efficiency and adaptability and (3) shows empirical evidence of social-behavioral underpinning on procedural accuracy, safety outcomes and energy efficiency over non-predictive systems. The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents related work in AR for clinical applications, Section 3 describes the AR-ClinAgent approach, Section 4 explains details on experimental set-up and evaluation measures that were used, Section 5 reports on results and discussion while section concludes with overview of our findings and future research directions. II Literature Review Augmented reality (AR) has gained attention of late in terms of improving precision during surgery and minimizing operative accidents. Stewart et al. (2022) found that 3D AR headsets enabled in-room robotic assistants were able to decrease the time of task completion and error rates, allowing non-expert staff to perform at the level of attending surgeons [1]. These results reinforce the idea of AR skill augmentation and assistance during complex intracorporeal procedures. In orthopedic surgery, AR imaging technologies also enhanced task efficiency and reduced cognitive load. Furman and Hsu (2021) investigated applications such as pedicle screw insertion and found improved operative accuracy with a reduction in radiation exposure in pre-clinical models, but acknowledged that clinical use would still be technology dependent based on user learning curve and procedural complexity [2]. Outside of the operating room, AR has penetrated rehabilitation and telemedicine. Yang et al. (2022) developed a hybrid AR-based VR rehabilitation system for stroke patients, which reduced human trainer burden and contact rates though gained functional improvement were significant [3]. Gouda et al. The existing AR-assisted systems are mostly centered around a single-procedure application and pre-clinical validation, and the standard for evaluating performance across various high-stakes clinical scenarios is still immature [1][2][5][6]. Although AI integration has enhanced predictive monitoring, diagnostic assistance and procedural effectiveness, we have not seen any solutions that bring together pro-active risk prediction, multi-agent coordination and real/pseudo-real time AR guidance in one coherent

segments.text: system [8][9][14][15]. Additionally, albeit other emerging fields such as telerehabilitation, space medicine and extreme environment applications, the potential for AR in remote guidance would be beneficial, there are still limitations with lack of measurable real - time performance assessment (other than qualitative user feedback), reproducible benchmarks or privacy-comtrait datasets to train / evaluate on [3][11][12][16]. The majority of academic, education-oriented VR/AR content does not assess real-time training outcomes such as safety outcomes, procedural latencies or energy efficiencies during experiential usage [13], [17]. Together these limitations underscore the lack of an overarching, standardized and scalable system that combines predictive intelligence, task allocation and AR-instrumented guidance in both standard practice and non-standardized clinical environments. Closing this gap is essential for the safety, reliability and regulatory readiness of AR-based health systems. III Methodology In this paper, we present AR-ClinAgent, a structured framework that combines Proactive Risk Anticipation (PRA) with Multi-Agent Orchestration to improve the performance of clinical AR assistants. The system builds upon a perceptor to effector loop that processes input and egocentric visual and sensor information, while mapping the latter into clinically validated procedural steps 19, by using a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mechanism. Specialised AI sub-agents are assigned specific cognitive tasks, such as path prediction, result validation and anomaly detection (see above), which enable task division to further optimise the latency and power over head without т compromising procedural realism [21]. Real-time AR views will be overlaid on the projected workflow to help clinicians through each step, and performance factors (such as accuracy of interventions being performed, number of interventions per individual imaged KE region and near misses) will be logged throughout for later review [22]. The approach uses privacy-preserving data across the range of human procedures, including ultrasound-guided IV access, central line insertion and medication verification to meet regulations while protecting patient health and safety. Simulation and manikin-based validation scenarios are used to compare baseline and PRA-amplified agent workflows, enabling reproducibility for comparisons with any future AR- assisted design [23]. segments.text: Figure 1: Layered Architecture of the AR-ClinAgent Framework for Proactive Clinical Workflow Assistance 3.1 Data Acquisition We used the Surgical Workflow and Activity Recognition Dataset (Cholec80) – a validated, publicly available video dataset of laparoscopic surgery for procedural understanding and automation [19]. It was chosen as it is a comprehensive dataset with high-quality visual data, and its surgical phases are well annotated to efficiently develop and evaluate AI guided AR systems. Cholec80 is a dataset of 80 laparoscopic cholecystectomy (gallbladder removal) videos, recorded at a resolution of 1920×1080 pixels, featuring synchronized metadata and extensive procedural annotations. These labels organize each surgery video into 7 different procedural phases: Preparation, Calot-Triangle Dissection, Clipping and Cutting, Gallbladder Dissectioning, Gallbladder Packaging, Cleaning/Clipping and Closing. Such frame-level annotation enables fine-grained temporal segmentation and contextual comprehension which are crucial for AR aided intraoperative guidance. The dataset was split into 64 (80%) videos for training and 16 videos (20%) for testing to be appropriately reflective of the number of each level-of-difficulty case available. The real-world nature of the dataset allows for training retrieval-augmented and explainable clinical agents aimed at precision guidance in a surgical setting whilst anticipating risk [20]. The Cholec80 videocine dataset produces multimodal data that is necessary for both spatial and temporal modeling. In addition, multiple videos are also accompanied by egocentric visual frames, tool presence annotations and timestamped procedural logs that serve as a parallel account of the surgical activity [21]. This architecture permits temporally synchronized integration of the visual and operational streams of data, which is imperative for the model to discover context-specific cues necessary for predictive clinical reasoning. Furthermore, sensor data within the laparoscopic instruments and embedded in the video metadata are used to assume motion dynamics, depth perception and instrument trajectory

The real time logging and online learning mechanism is an essential part of PRA that logs every near-miss event, every intervention requirement into a secure, privacy compliant event bank [37]. In addition, because of the continuous learning loops, PRA can automatically adjust its parameter setting by accumulating the longitudinal feedback, which increases its predictive accuracy for a wide range of procedural settings. By integrating probabilistic modeling, multi-agent data fusion and adaptive event logging the PRA module constitutes a major advancement beyond reactive safety approaches by incorporating proactive error handling. It not only predicts failure modes but also offers informative suggestions for how to improve clinical work-flow efficiency and with low cognitive burden. By integrating a risk prediction into the real-time guidance part of an AR system, trust, confidence and safety for the procedure are further enhanced with a network of checks that act as a kinetic shield against a medical workflow that evolves with sophistication [40]. The approach uses an organized set of performance metrics that assess procedural fidelity, response time, number and type of interventions, adverse events and energy usage to provide complete characterization of simulation-based learning and manikin-based practice [23]. segments.text: The results include the performance of AR-ClinAgent on a wide range of clinical and operational measures. It contrasts the proposed framework of PRA-augmented-based with state-of-the-art AR methods over both baseline and several existing AR-assisted architectures in terms of enhancing accuracy, safety, latency, as well as energy consumption. Simulations and manikin studies were included to promote generalizability and clinical applicability. The study emphasizes task-level and general procedural improvements facilitated by the combination of proactive intelligence, multi-agent orchestration and RAG-based procedural grounding. Figure 4: Comparative Evaluation of Step-Wise Accuracy, Clinical Interventions, Near-Miss Incidents, Latency, and Energy Usage Across AR-Assisted Models The performance comparison of AR-ClinAgent (PRA) with five other AR-assisted clinical models in terms of different evaluation measurements is depicted in Fig.[4]. AR-ClinAgent increases a step-wise execution accuracy of the intended treatments by 26%, decreases interventions with regard to clinical supervision by 31% and near miss events are reduced by 22% compared to baseline systems. Furthermore, there are reductions of 18% in latency and 14% of device-level energy consumption disparity, which demonstrate the efficiency and safety advantages with task-distributed AR guidance in procedural tasks.

segments.text: Figure 7: Holistic Multi-Metric Assessment of AR-Assisted Clinical Systems Using Normalized Performance Indicators Figure 7 presents an overall picture of AR-ClinAgent (PRA) in light of all criteria. Step-wise execution accuracy is improved by 26%, clinical interventions are reduced by 31%, near-misses decrease by 22%, latency improves by 18% and energy is conserved up to 14%. The figure highlights that the model can find a trade-off between procedural accuracy, safety and process efficiency better than the other Classic AR-assisted systems performed on five different working scenarios. 5.1 Ablation Study To investigate the endowment of each component in AR-ClinAgent, we performed an ablation study. Three major properties, namely Proactive Risk Anticipation (PRA), Multi-Agent Orchestration (MAO) and RAG based procedural grounding, were incrementally eliminated to examine their contributions to system performance. The authors assessed temporal accuracy, levels of interspersed clinical interventions, near-misses, lead-lag times and energy for each set-up. We find that removal of PRA induced a more significant reduction in safety indices than MAO exclusion, whereas MAO exclusion caused mainly additional latency and energy. The lack of RAG grounding resulted in some inaccuracy in step-by-step execution, demonstrating the necessity of RAG element for aligning AR guidance onto evidence-based clinical workflow. This examination also seemed to suggest that each of the components contributed independently (uniquely) both to efficiency of use and clinical safety.

The achievement rate of execution step has the largest reduction without RAG grounding and also latency and energy consumption are increased significantly for MAO removal, and safety is deteriorated for PRA removal. Results validate the significance of individual mechanical components in terms of effectiveness and safety for clinical practice. 5.2 Discussion The evaluation of AR-ClinAgent demonstrates that the integration of PRA, MAO and RAG in procedural grounding allows for significant improvements over clinical safety and operational efficiency. The PRA significantly cuts down by 22%, the proportion of near misses and clinical oversight interventions by 31%, confirming the necessity and benefits of predictive error detection in complex procedural tasks. MAO to sub-agents and splitting the computation load MAO is less latent by 18% and consumes (device-level energy consumption) less energy by 14%, this provides a good insight of gains in efficiency when employing levels of intelligent task allocation. RAG- based grounding provides a 26% improvement in step-wise procedural accuracy, justifying its capacity to bring AR guidance closer to a protocol scrutinised by clinicians. Comparison with other AR-enhanced models demonstrates that AR-ClinAgent surpasses state-of-the-art systems on all the major indicators, demonstrating the synergistic power of predictive intelligence, structured multi-agent coordination and procedural grounding. These findings demonstrate that AR-ClinAgent is not only helpful in assisting clinicians to follow the prescribed procedure accurately but also in improving the resource efficiency, so that it can be scaled up to use cases of simulation labs, manikin-based training and real-world clinician environment. VI Conclusion The AR-ClinAgent framework coupled with a set of PRA, MAO and RAG-based procedural grounding shows significant gains in the efficiency, accuracy and safety of clinical workflow. Baseline studies demonstrate that, compared with non-predictive AR systems, clinical

segments.text: oversight interventions can be reduced by 31%, step-wise execution accuracy improved by 26% and near-misses cut by 22% using AR-ClinAgent. Moreover, 18% of instruction accessed latency can be saved and device level energy consumption is improved with 14% through task-distributed processing to increase not only the efficiency of work in operation but also that resources are utilized. The intuitive interface of the system supports several procedural tasks and displays depth-aware AR overlays with occlusion to a minimal extent such that it would be readable for clinicians. The multi-agent coordination enables the splitting of cognitive load between sub-agents specialised in, e.g., step prognostics, error verification and outcome validation. Procedural grounding with the RAG-based clinician-validated knowledge aligns the system well with real clinical practices, and thus enhances the decision quality. The evaluation experiment of simulation and manikin scenarios indicates the repeatability, security, as well as scalability of AR-ClinAgent. Its novel anticipated insight with semi-automatic AR guidance leads to addressing important limitations among existing AR-based clinical tools. For the next stage development, expansion of datasets diversity, integration with the patient-specific physiology modelling and extension to real-world clinical validation are means for enhancing applicability and generalisation potential of AR-ClinAgent under a wide variety of healthcare situations.
